newsitem.title: PERU: Peru crash inquiry focuses on computer glitch.
newsitem.headline: Peru crash inquiry focuses on computer glitch.

text.p: Experts on Thursday began to investigate the crash of a Boeing 757-200 in the Peruvian Pacific, killing all 70 on board, which the government has blamed on a computer malfunction.

"It is not the first time that one of these planes has had this kind of fault," Transport Minister Elsa Carrera de Escalante told a news conference. "We have to find out why the computers went crazy."

A group of around 12 investigators from Boeing, engine maker Pratt & Whitney, the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transporation Safety Board met with representatives from Aeroperu, the local airline that owned the plane.

Boeing's spokesman in Seattle, Russ Young, told Reuters it was "too early to even guess" what happened to the plane which, according to President Alberto Fujimori, had only been in service for three months.
Carrera said the inquiry would centre on computer failure aboard the jet, a theory based on recordings of a dramatic, 29-minute dialogue between pilot Eric Schreiber and Lima air control.

"We've lost the basic instruments, both for height and for speed ... I've cut back the engines but we are accelerating," Schreiber said, according to Carrera. "Where am I? Over land or sea?" The minister said Schreiber spoke with "incredible" calm as he tried to head back to Lima through dense fog.
Young said Schreiber's last words with Lima's air traffic control would provide important clues for the investigation.

Carrera added the government had asked for U.S. help to recover the aircraft's two "black box" flight recorders, which were believed trapped inside the plane's trunk 180 yards (164.6 metres) below the sea surface.
The Peruvian navy continued to scour the crash site for debris and bodies on Thursday.

Using helicopters, navy frigates and various private boats, rescuers had plucked 14 bodies from the icy waters by Thursday evening, along with clothing, shoes and fragments of the plane's wing and fuselage.
"The problem is that the central part of the fuselage is too deep," said navy captain Augusto Zegarra, adding that most of the bodies were still trapped in the wreckage.
Meanwhile, relatives of the victims, who came from 11 countries, were arriving in Peru on Thursday to identify the few bodies already recovered and visit the site.

Condolences poured in from around the world, including Pope John Paul II, French President Jacques Chirac, and the government of neighbouring Chile, which lost 30 people in the crash. A mass was to be held on Thursday night for the victims.

Wednesday's crash, one of the worst in Peru's aviation history, came seven months after a Boeing 737 belonging to the local airline Faucett crashed and killed all 123 people on board near Peru's second city, Arequipa.
Since 1967, a total of 601 people have been killed in air crashes in Peru. Aeroperu, privatised in 1993 and 100 percent owned by Aeromexico, was operating flights normally on Thursday.

The crash was the third involving a 757, which had a perfect safety record from the time it entered commercial service in 1983 until last year, when an American Airlines jet slammed into a mountain in Colombia, killing 159 people.
In February, a 757-200 crashed into the Caribbean shortly after taking off from the Dominican Republic, killing all 189 people aboard. Both crashes were blamed on pilot error.
